title: Vividly Visualize Accomplishments the Team Is Far From Attaining
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article makes the case that visualization is a leadership tool, not just a motivational cliche, because turning a distant goal into a vivid mental picture helps teams see the steps required to get there. It offers storyboards, vision boards, and role-play as concrete tactics, and uses college basketball coach Jim Valvano's practice of cutting down the nets before ever winning a championship as its central example. The author argues that making success feel real, well before it's achieved, builds the emotional commitment needed to sustain a long effort. The piece closes by tying vivid imagery directly to team alignment and motivation.
points: Visualization converts abstract, distant goals into concrete expectations and intentions
Storyboards, roadmaps, vision boards, and role-play can make a far-off accomplishment feel real
Jim Valvano had his team practice cutting down championship nets long before they won the title
Vivid images of success build the emotional commitment needed for a long, difficult effort
quotes: By visualizing the accomplishment, even those far in the distance, leaders turn abstract and wishful goals into expectations and intentions.
The more vivid the visual, the more engaged people become. Good leaders make the pathway to success vividly clear.
He insisted they do this in early team practices so they could visualize the pride and satisfaction of what winning would feel like.
Visualizing successful completion highlights the significance and meaning of success.
If the goal is big and meaty, visualizing the accomplishment will help align the team and inspire engagement and action.
